deep_dive_html:
The Manufacturing CAM Trap: Capital Expenditure Leakage

In industrial and manufacturing leases, Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clauses are rarely just about landscaping and snow removal. For manufacturing tenants, the true danger lies in the ambiguity surrounding 'repair' versus 'replacement' of heavy-intensive infrastructure. Landlords frequently draft CAM provisions that permit the pass-through of capital expenditures—such as the complete resurfacing of heavy-duty reinforced concrete pads, the replacement of industrial-grade dock levelers, or the upgrading of specialized drainage systems—under the guise of routine maintenance.

When a landlord classifies a structural replacement as an operating expense, they are effectively forcing the tenant to subsidize the long-term appreciation of the landlord's asset. This is particularly predatory in manufacturing, where the high-impact nature of operations can be used as a pretext to justify frequent, high-cost 'repairs' that are actually fundamental capital improvements. Furthermore, landlords often include 'uncontrollable expenses' clauses that allow them to pass through utility spikes or tax reassessments without any ceiling on the total increase.

Market-Standard Protections for Industrial Tenants

To protect your manufacturing margins, your lease must strictly differentiate between operational maintenance and capital improvements. An elite-scale negotiation should focus on the following three pillars of protection:

  • Amortization Requirements: If a capital improvement is permitted to be passed through, the cost must be amortized over its useful life according to GAAP standards, with only the portion applicable to the current lease term charged to the tenant. This prevents a single year of massive, unbudgeted expense.
  • Explicit CapEx Exclusions: The CAM definition must explicitly exclude structural repairs, roof replacements, and the replacement of heavy-duty utility infrastructure unless such replacements are necessitated by the tenant's specific gross negligence.
  • Audit and Verification Rights: Tenants must retain the right to audit landlord's books to ensure that 'administrative fees' or 'management fees' are not being inflated to cover the landlord's internal overhead or non-related property costs.
  • Expense Caps: Negotiate a 'cap' on the year-over-year increase of controllable CAM expenses to ensure predictable operational budgeting.

Beyond physical infrastructure, beware of 'administrative markups.' Many landlords attempt to add a percentage-based fee on top of third-party vendor invoices for repairs. Without a strict prohibition on such markups, you are essentially paying a hidden tax on every repair performed on the property.
